extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and students of poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for poetic diction, choice of subject, character-representation, metrical practice, and use of rustic or colloquial language in poetry. Emphasises how metre and poetic aims constrain diction and character-language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality of imagery and thought vs common tropes
rubrics_metrics.description: "The imagery is almost always general: sun, moon, flowers, breezes, murmuring streams, warbling songsters... are the materials which are common to all, and which each shaped and arranged according to his judgment or fancy"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying solely on conventional, general images. While earlier poets achieved charm by arrangement and polish, modern excellence should combine such finish with "keener interest, deeper pathos, and the fresher and more various imagery". Anti-pattern: uncritical recycling of mythological or stock images without novel treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exquisite polish of diction combined with perfect simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: The excellence aimed at by older poets consisted in "the exquisite polish of the diction, combined with perfect simplicity."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pursue polished diction that is also simple: avoid words a gentleman would not use in dignified conversation and words only a learned man would use. Arrange words so each part is melodious in itself and contributes to the harmony of the whole. Scoring note: harmony and simplicity of diction are central measures of poetic craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Melodious arrangement and metrical variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Studied position of words and phrases so "not only each part should be melodious in itself, but contribute to the harmony of the whole... and lastly with equal labour... the variation and various harmonies of their metrical movement."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on local melodiousness and how phrases conduct to surrounding words; employ subtle metrical variations rather than clumsy novelty. Anti-pattern: meters that impose "a specific overpowering tune" causing readers to favour sound over sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety via modification of common metres, not forced foreign metres
rubrics_metrics.description: Elder bards produced "a far greater as well as more charming variety by countless modifications, and subtle balances of sound in the common metres of their country" rather than introducing new metres "borrowed from the German" which may have an "overpowering tune."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek variety by skilful modification of familiar meters. Beware importing meters whose mechanical rhythm drowns sense (example criticism: Alonzo and Imogen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Union of classical finish with modern depth and imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: A lasting reputation awaits the man who should "recall the high finish... and above all, the perfusive and omnipresent grace" of classical poets and "combine the keener interest, deeper pathos, manlier reflection, and the fresher and more various imagery" of modern poets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to blend classical technical virtues (finish, appropriateness, proportion) with modern strengths (pathos, reflection, fresh imagery). This union is presented as an ideal standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of subject-matter: rustic life is not universally suitable
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule that "the proper diction for poetry in general consists altogether in a language taken... from the mouths of men in real life" is applicable only to certain classes of poetry and is not generally practicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume low and rustic life is the proper source for poetic diction in all poetry. Use subject-matter (e.g., rustic life) only when it genuinely serves the poem's aims; otherwise it may be useless or injurious to general poetic diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as essentially ideal and generic
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopts Aristotle's principle "that poetry, as poetry, is essentially ideal, that it avoids and excludes all accident; that its apparent individualities of rank, character, or occupation must be representative of a class; and that the persons of poetry must be clothed with generic attributes."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters in poetry should embody class-generic attributes rather than idiosyncratic particulars. The poetic person must be probable as a representative of his class, not merely an individual exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verisimilitude through class-appropriate manners and sentiments
rubrics_metrics.description: "The characters... have all the verisimilitude and representative quality, that the purposes of poetry can require. They are persons of a known and abiding class, and their manners and sentiments the natural product of circumstances common to the class."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure a character's behaviour, feelings, and language plausibly flow from circumstances typical of their class. Example: Coleridge's reading of Michael as possessing such verisimilitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selectivity in adopting rustic traits — need for prior education or sensibility
rubrics_metrics.description: To prosper in rustic life a certain vantage-ground is prerequisite: "Education, or original sensibility, or both, must pre-exist, if the changes, forms, and incidents of nature are to prove a sufficient stimulant."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When representing rustic characters who display reflective feeling, justify it by antecedent causes (education, sensibility). Avoid assuming rustic surroundings alone produce reflective poetic sensibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid literal imitation of dull or garrulous speech in lyric poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: In a lyric poem "it is not possible to imitate truly a dull and garrulous discourser, without repeating the effects of dullness and garrulity."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious when adopting a narrator's voice that is inherently dull or garrulous—such faithful imitation can degrade the poem. When necessary, supply introductory context or let poetical passages come from the poet's voice rather than attempting full verbal mimicry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide context when using a distinct narrator-persona
rubrics_metrics.description: In THE THORN the poet "acknowledges in a note the necessity of an introductory poem, in which he should have portrayed the character of the person from whom the words of the poem are supposed to proceed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you adopt a narrowly characterized persona (with odd speech or beliefs), furnish introductory material to orient the reader and prevent misreadings or unintended disgust. Anti-pattern: dropping a speaker into a poem without setting expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unintended grotesque associations when depicting infirmity
rubrics_metrics.description: Charge against THE IDIOT BOY: "the author has not... taken sufficient care to preclude from the reader’s fancy the disgusting images of ordinary morbid idiocy..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When portraying mental or physical infirmity, guard against summoning grotesque or repulsive images that contradict the poem's intended pathos; use counterbalancing description (e.g., of beauty) where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rustic vocabulary alone does not constitute the 'best part' of language
rubrics_metrics.description: The best parts of language are "the product of philosophers, not of clowns or shepherds" and are "derived from reflection on the acts of the mind itself."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying solely on rustic terms limits expressive range; cultivate vocabulary capable of expressing abstract and reflective mental processes. The poet should draw on the fuller resources of language, not only colloquial rural speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rustic speech must be purified and reconstructed for poetic use
rubrics_metrics.description: "A rustic’s language, purified from all provincialism and grossness, and so far reconstructed as to be made consistent with the rules of grammar... will not differ from the language of any other man of common sense..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using colloquial or regional speech, expect to alter and refine it substantially (remove provincialisms, fix grammar) before it serves in poetry. The necessary omissions and changes are often "numerous and weighty."

rubrics_metrics.name: No essential identity between prose and metrical composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Countering Wordsworth: "Between the language of prose and that of metrical composition, there neither is, nor can be, any essential difference:" Coleridge objects and argues for a difference in ordonnance and style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat poetic diction and prose diction as distinct: metre, ordering, and poetic style impose conditions not present in ordinary prose. The poet should not assume prose idiom is fully adequate for metrical composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metre imposes necessary consequences on diction and word-order
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter XVIII: "Origin and elements of metre—Its necessary consequences, and the conditions thereby imposed on the metrical writer in the choice of his diction."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose words and order with metrical constraints in mind. Metrical composition demands different arrangements and often different choices of words than prose to fulfill rhythmical and melodic requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic selection presupposes possession of language and judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: "The very power of making the selection implies the previous possession of the language selected... We do not adopt the language of a class by the mere adoption of such words exclusively... but likewise by following the order, in which the words of such men are wont to succeed each other."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poet must possess and command language and ordering patterns before effectively adopting or imitating a class-dialect; mere word-lifting without mastery of ordering yields inauthentic results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orderliness and prospectiveness of thought reflected in diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Uneducated intercourse is "distinguished... by the greater disjunction and separation in the component parts of that... which they wish to communicate. There is a want of that prospectiveness of mind, that surview, which enables a man to foresee the whole... and by this means so to subordinate and arrange the different parts... as to convey it at once, and as an organized whole."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetic diction should demonstrate intellectual prospectiveness and subordinated arrangement—words and clauses arranged to reveal a coherent organized thought. Avoid the disjoined, piecemeal ordering characteristic of unreflective conversation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition as legitimate poetic device when reflecting sustained passion
rubrics_metrics.description: "Such repetitions I admit to be a beauty of the highest kind; as illustrated by Mr. Wordsworth himself from the song of Deborah. 'At her feet he bowed, he fell, he lay down...'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repetition deliberately to reflect persistent or intense feeling; it can be among the highest beauties of poetic diction when it mirrors the nature of passion or sustained emphasis. Distinguish such purposeful repeating from the aimless fillers of unfurnished speech.
